_meta.source: Standard CBT framework (D. Burns 'Feeling Good' 10 distortions, extended); ids match the Chinese file for code parity.

cognitive_distortions.name: Catastrophizing
cognitive_distortions.definition: Imagining small problems or uncertain outcomes as full-blown disasters.
examples: If I bomb tomorrow's presentation, my career is over.
If I don't sleep tonight, tomorrow will be a complete disaster.
If I lose this job, I'll never work again.
socratic_questions: If the worst really did happen, what's the most likely actual consequence?
Even in the worst case, is there a chance it's not as bad as it feels right now?
Have you been through anything like this before? How did it actually turn out?
If a friend were in this exact situation, what would you say to them?
A month from now, will this still feel like a disaster?
What's the evidence this is truly catastrophic? What's the evidence against?
cognitive_distortions.reframing: Uncertainty is not the same as catastrophe. Even the worst outcome is rarely the end of the world.

cognitive_distortions.name: All-or-Nothing Thinking
cognitive_distortions.definition: Evaluating situations in extreme, binary terms with no middle ground.
examples: Either I do this perfectly, or I'm a failure.
If I disagree with him at all, I'm not supporting him.
Either I'm all in, or I should give up entirely.
socratic_questions: Is there any possibility between these two extremes?
What's the territory between 'perfect' and 'failure'?
If you had to grade yourself, would it really be 0 or 100?
Can something be 'okay but not great' and still count?
Does one outcome really define your entire worth?
cognitive_distortions.reframing: Most of life lives in shades of gray. The middle ground is where most real outcomes actually sit.

cognitive_distortions.name: Mind Reading
cognitive_distortions.definition: Assuming you know what others are thinking, with no real evidence.
examples: He must think I'm incompetent.
My boss definitely sees me as a liability.
I know everyone is talking about me behind my back.
socratic_questions: How could you actually know what they're thinking?
Is it possible they're thinking something completely different?
Even if they were thinking that, is their thought the same as fact?
Have you ever been wrong about what someone was thinking?
What's the evidence — beyond a feeling — that this is what they think?
cognitive_distortions.reframing: We can't know what's in someone else's head unless they tell us. Assumption is not the same as fact.

cognitive_distortions.name: Overgeneralization
cognitive_distortions.definition: Drawing a universal negative conclusion from a single event.
examples: I always mess things up.
I never do anything right.
Everyone always lets me down.
socratic_questions: Does one failure really speak for every time?
Is there even one small thing you didn't mess up recently?
Are words like 'always' and 'never' really accurate here?
Does this single outcome really generalize to everything else?
If you collected the actual evidence, would the conclusion still hold?
cognitive_distortions.reframing: A single event is one data point, not a verdict. Looking for counter-examples helps see the fuller picture.

cognitive_distortions.name: Personalization
cognitive_distortions.definition: Holding yourself responsible for events that are only partly — or not at all — within your control.
examples: He's in a bad mood — it must be because of me.
The project failed because I wasn't good enough.
If I'd been a better partner, we wouldn't be fighting.
socratic_questions: What other factors might have contributed to this?
Do you really control every variable here?
If a friend were in this exact spot, would you blame them?
Is it possible this has nothing to do with you at all?
Are you taking responsibility that isn't actually yours to carry?
cognitive_distortions.reframing: Many things have many causes. You may be one of several factors — not the whole reason.

cognitive_distortions.name: Mental Filter
cognitive_distortions.definition: Focusing only on negative details and filtering out all positive evidence.
examples: Today was just one bad thing after another.
There is nothing good about this job.
Sure they praised me, but it still doesn't feel like enough.
socratic_questions: Was there even one moment today that went okay?
If you listed everything that happened, what's the ratio of negative to positive?
Why doesn't the positive thing deserve the same attention?
What's the filter you're using to decide what counts?
If a friend only remembered today's bad parts, what would you say to them?
cognitive_distortions.reframing: Negative things happened — and they're not the whole story. Naming positives helps keep balance.

cognitive_distortions.name: Mind as Reality
cognitive_distortions.definition: Treating your thoughts and intuitions as objective facts about the world.
examples: I have a feeling this will go wrong — so it will.
I feel like I'm not competent, so I must not be.
I'm scared of speaking in public, so I'm going to humiliate myself.
socratic_questions: Is a feeling the same thing as a fact?
Have you ever had a 'gut sense' that turned out to be wrong?
What's the difference between 'I feel X' and 'X is true'?
Without this thought, would you see the situation differently?
Can we separate 'I'm afraid this will happen' from 'this will actually happen'?
cognitive_distortions.reframing: Thoughts are thoughts. They are real as experiences, but they aren't evidence.

cognitive_distortions.name: Emotional Reasoning
cognitive_distortions.definition: Using your emotional state as proof that something is objectively true.
examples: I feel guilty, so I must have done something wrong.
I feel inadequate, so I must really be inadequate.
I feel this much anxiety — something dangerous must be happening.
socratic_questions: Does guilt always mean you actually did something wrong?
Can emotion be a signal without being a verdict?
If you didn't feel this way, would the objective facts of the situation change?
Can you say 'I feel...' instead of 'I am...'?
When we're afraid, doesn't a lot of stuff look more dangerous than it really is?
cognitive_distortions.reframing: Feelings are signals, not verdicts. They're real, but they aren't logic.

cognitive_distortions.name: Should Statements
cognitive_distortions.definition: Using rigid 'should' / 'must' / 'ought to' rules to demand things of yourself or others.
examples: I should always be the strongest one.
I shouldn't feel sad about this.
I should be able to handle everything on my own.
socratic_questions: Whose rule is this, really?
Is this 'should' reasonable? Are there exceptions?
If a friend held themselves to this rule, what would you tell them?
What changes if you swap 'should' for 'I'd like to'?
Are humans actually capable of always doing this?
cognitive_distortions.reframing: Trading 'I should' for 'I'd like to' or 'It would help if I' lowers the pressure of self-criticism.

cognitive_distortions.name: Labeling
cognitive_distortions.definition: Defining yourself or someone else entirely by one negative label.
examples: I'm just a failure.
He's a selfish person.
I'm so stupid — I can't do anything right.
socratic_questions: Can one event define an entire person?
If a friend labeled themselves this way, what would you say?
Can any human be summed up in one word?
Can you describe the behavior instead of giving yourself a label?
What's the difference between 'I'm a failure' and 'I failed at this one thing'?
cognitive_distortions.reframing: Describe behavior, not identity. Behaviors are specific and changeable; labels are sweeping and usually unfair.

cognitive_distortions.name: Fortune Telling
cognitive_distortions.definition: Predicting negative future outcomes as if they were already certain.
examples: I know tomorrow is going to be awful.
This is definitely going to fail.
We're not going to get along — I can already tell.
socratic_questions: How confident can you really be about the future?
Have you predicted things before that didn't come true?
Are you predicting, or are you worrying?
If you let the prediction go, what would you actually see?
Is 'most likely outcome' the same as 'worst possible outcome'?
cognitive_distortions.reframing: The future hasn't happened yet. Your prediction is one possibility, not a guarantee.

cognitive_distortions.name: Disqualifying the Positive
cognitive_distortions.definition: Rejecting or dismissing positive experiences and achievements, deciding they 'don't count.'
examples: It was just luck — it doesn't say anything about my ability.
Anyone could have done that. It's no big deal.
I might have succeeded this time, but I won't next time.
socratic_questions: Do you really believe that was only luck?
Is it possible your effort and skill also played a role?
If your best friend had this success, what would you say to them?
Why do you hold yourself to a different standard than others?
Can you accept the simple statement: 'I did well this time'?
cognitive_distortions.reframing: Positive experiences are real. Letting them count is itself a skill worth practicing.

cognitive_distortions.name: Magnification / Minimization
cognitive_distortions.definition: Inflating the importance of negative events while shrinking positives.
examples: If I don't sleep tonight, tomorrow is ruined.
Yes I learned a lot, but that one failure is what really matters.
This small win doesn't really matter.
socratic_questions: Does one bad night really ruin everything?
Let's weigh it: one rough night vs. all the nights you've handled okay — are they really the same weight?
What if we let the positive thing be a little bigger too?
If we shrink the negative back to actual size, is it still that scary?
What scale are you using to decide what's big and what's small?
cognitive_distortions.reframing: Let's put things at the right scale. One thing mattering doesn't mean another thing matters less.

cognitive_distortions.name: Lack of Coping Belief
cognitive_distortions.definition: Assuming you can't handle a difficult situation, even when there's evidence you can.
examples: There's no way I can handle this.
This is too much. I can't do it.
No one can help — I just have to suffer through it alone.
socratic_questions: Have you handled anything similar before? Even something small?
If the worst really did happen, are you sure there's nothing you could do?
When you feel you 'just have to bear it,' what are you actually doing in practice?
Could asking for help itself be a form of coping?
If your best friend were here, would you assume they couldn't handle it?
cognitive_distortions.reframing: You're already coping with more than you give yourself credit for. Denying that doesn't make it less true.
detection_keywords: i just have to bear it

cognitive_distortions.name: Regretful Thinking
cognitive_distortions.definition: Focusing on what was lost or missed, while ignoring what you still have.
examples: If only I'd taken the other job.
If only I'd tried harder back then.
I missed my chance.
socratic_questions: What do you have right now that's worth being grateful for?
If you could choose again, do you really know which path would have been better?
Does regret change the past, or just consume the present?
What if you put the energy you spend regretting into what you can do now?
Standing here today, was that past choice really completely wrong?
cognitive_distortions.reframing: The past can't change, but the choices you made shaped who you are now. Focus on what you can use today.
